title: Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (MIME) Part Five: Conformance Criteria and Examples
summary: The fifth and final MIME document. It describes MIME conformance criteria and gives examples of MIME messages, along with acknowledgements and the bibliography.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2049 defines the minimum behavior of a mail program that claims MIME conformance. It also explains how to prepare message content and what changes it may face while traveling through email systems.

questions: what must a mime compliant mail client do
what is the mime canonical encoding model
why do email gateways corrupt messages
why can email gateways alter message content
subtitle: Minimum MIME mail-agent requirements, email transport cautions, and an encoding model.

tldr.problem: MIME mail can contain many kinds of content, but not every mail program can handle every type, and mail can be altered by gateways in transit.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines ten minimum requirements for MIME-conformant user agents, gives eight cautions for data sent through mail, and describes a four-step canonical encoding model.
tldr.outcome: A conformant agent can safely treat unknown content as opaque data rather than display it as text. RFC 2049 obsoletes RFC 1521, RFC 1522, and RFC 1590.

facts.label: Long lines that may be altered

today: RFC 2049 is a Draft Standard published in November 1996 and obsoletes RFC 1521, RFC 1522, and RFC 1590. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Where This Document Fits
sections.content:
RFC 2049 is the fifth and final document in the Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (MIME) set. MIME lets email carry text in different character sets, non-text content, multipart bodies, and non-ASCII text in headers.

This part defines MIME conformance, describes transport problems, and presents a canonical encoding model. It also includes a complex multipart example and a summary of changes from earlier MIME documents.
sections.plainLanguage: MIME is a set of rules for carrying different kinds of content in email. This final part sets a minimum for mail programs and explains how message content is prepared for transfer.

sections.title: What MIME-Conformant Agents Must Do
sections.content:
A MIME-conformant mail user agent need not support every media type, but it must safely handle content it does not recognize. It generates a MIME-Version: 1.0 header, recognizes transfer encodings, interprets Content-Type, and avoids displaying non-text data as raw text.

For unknown content types or encodings, the agent treats the data as application/octet-stream. It also recognizes multipart/mixed, multipart/alternative, multipart/digest, and message/rfc822, and follows the specified fallback behavior for unknown subtypes.

The requirements also cover non-ASCII text and encoded words in headers. The RFC describes this minimum as safe because unfamiliar data can be kept as undifferentiated binary rather than shown as text.
sections.plainLanguage: A conformant mail program identifies message content and decodes the transfer formats it supports. When it does not recognize content, it treats it as data rather than showing it as text.

sections.title: Content That May Change in Transit
sections.content:
Email may pass through network systems that do not preserve every byte or formatting choice. The RFC advises senders not to rely on isolated carriage returns or line feeds, NUL bytes, tabs, trailing spaces, or lines longer than 76 characters being preserved.

It also identifies 73 characters that are known to remain consistent across character-converting gateways: letters, digits, and eleven special characters. A period alone on a line and a line beginning with From may also be corrupted by some mail systems.

These are cautions about known failures, not recommended behavior for mail servers. The RFC says transport agents should not alter whitespace or wrap long lines.
sections.plainLanguage: Some mail systems alter content as they transfer it. Senders should avoid relying on characters and line formats that gateways may change.

sections.title: The Four-Step Encoding Model
sections.content:
The RFC models MIME composition as four steps for each innermost body. First create the content in its local form; next convert it to the canonical form for its media type; then apply a transfer encoding; finally add MIME headers and insert the entity into a message or multipart body.

For text/plain, canonical form uses a supported character set and CRLF line endings. The appropriate transfer encoding depends on the body; there is no fixed mapping from media type to encoding.

These steps describe a model, not required internal software architecture. Implementations may combine or add processing steps, but their resulting messages must be consistent with the model.
sections.plainLanguage: MIME prepares each body by converting it to a standard form, applying a transfer encoding, and adding headers. A receiving program reverses those steps, though the resulting local form may differ from the original.

sections.title: A Nested Multipart Message
sections.content:
The appendix outlines a message with five parts: two introductory text parts, a nested multipart, a text/enriched part, and a message/rfc822 part. The nested multipart contains audio and a JPEG image intended to be presented in parallel.

The example also shows that a multipart message can contain a preamble, parts without explicit headers, and an encapsulated message with its own character set and transfer encoding. A MIME-aware reader ignores the preamble.
sections.plainLanguage: The example shows that a message can contain several parts and nested containers. Each part can have its own content type and transfer encoding.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RFC 2049 does not define a separate security mechanism. It directs readers to the MIME media types document, RFC 2046, for security issues.

One conformance requirement limits accidental exposure: an agent avoids displaying raw data of a type it does not understand and treats it as opaque binary content.
sections.plainLanguage: Security details are discussed in another MIME document. The conformance rules here help prevent unknown binary data from being displayed as text.

items.title: 1. Local form
items.text: Content begins in the system's native format.

items.title: 2. Canonical form
items.text: Convert it to the standard form for its media type.

items.title: 3. Transfer encoding
items.text: Apply an encoding such as Base64 or quoted-printable.

items.title: 4. Entity insertion
items.text: Add MIME headers and place it in a message or multipart body.
